description: Brain lobes, cerebellum, localisation of function, and Penfield's interpretive cortex study.
content_html:
Structure of the Brain

The brain is the most complex organ in the human body. Psychologists divide it into regions to understand which parts are responsible for which functions — a principle called localisation of function. The outer surface of the brain, the cerebral cortex, is divided into four main lobes, each with distinct roles.

The Four Lobes

The frontal lobe sits at the front of the brain. It contains the motor cortex, which controls voluntary movement, and the prefrontal cortex, which is involved in planning, decision-making and personality. Damage to the frontal lobe can change personality and affect self-control, as illustrated by the famous historical case of Phineas Gage.

The temporal lobe is located at the sides of the brain, roughly behind the ears. It processes sounds and contains Wernicke’s area, which is crucial for understanding spoken and written language. The temporal lobe is also involved in memory consolidation.

The parietal lobe lies behind the frontal lobe and above the temporal lobe. It contains the somatosensory cortex, which receives and processes information from the skin, muscles and joints — allowing you to feel touch, temperature and pain.

The occipital lobe is at the back of the brain. It is entirely dedicated to visual processing. The primary visual cortex receives signals from the eyes, and surrounding areas interpret colour, movement and shape.

The cerebellum is a cauliflower-like structure at the back and base of the brain. It coordinates smooth, precise movement and balance. Without the cerebellum, actions such as catching a ball or writing would become clumsy and uncoordinated. It also plays a role in procedural learning — acquiring motor skills through practice.

Key Fact

The four lobes: frontal (front, movement + planning), temporal (sides, hearing + language), parietal (top-back, touch + senses), occipital (back, vision). The cerebellum (base-back) coordinates movement and balance.

Localisation of Function

Within each lobe, specific areas have specific functions. The motor area (primary motor cortex) in the frontal lobe controls voluntary movement. The somatosensory area in the parietal lobe processes touch and body sensation. These two areas run as parallel strips separated by a groove called the central sulcus.

The visual area in the occipital lobe processes sight; the auditory area in the temporal lobe processes sound. Language is handled by two key areas: Broca’s area in the frontal lobe controls speech production, while Wernicke’s area in the temporal lobe is involved in language comprehension.

Aim: Wilder Penfield aimed to map the functions of the cortex in patients undergoing brain surgery for epilepsy, to understand which areas controlled movement, sensation and conscious experience.

Method: During surgery, Penfield applied a small electrical probe to specific areas of the cortex in patients who were kept awake under local anaesthetic. The patients could report what they experienced as each area was stimulated. Penfield carefully recorded which physical movement or sensation resulted from stimulating each point.

Results: Stimulating the motor cortex caused involuntary movements in specific body parts, producing a systematic map of the body across the cortex — now called the motor homunculus. Stimulating the temporal lobe caused patients to report vivid memories, sounds and experiences, suggesting this region has a role in conscious experience. Penfield called this region the “interpretive cortex.”

Conclusion: The cortex is systematically organised, with different areas responsible for different functions. The temporal lobe in particular appeared to be involved in interpreting and replaying past experiences, providing early evidence that specific functions are localised to specific brain areas.

Key Fact

Penfield mapped the cortex by electrically stimulating the brains of awake epilepsy patients during surgery. Stimulating the motor cortex caused body movements; stimulating the temporal lobe triggered vivid memories. His conclusion was that cortical functions are localised — different areas control different behaviours.

A strength of the localisation of function idea is that it is supported by consistent evidence from multiple sources: Penfield’s electrical stimulation, case studies of brain-damaged patients, and modern brain scanning studies all point to the same organisational principle.

However, localisation has limits. Many complex behaviours — language, emotion, memory — involve networks of brain areas rather than a single region. Brain plasticity research shows that after injury, healthy parts of the brain can sometimes take over functions previously performed by damaged areas, suggesting the brain is more flexible than a strict localisation view implies.
exam_tip_html: For questions on Penfield’s study, always cover all four elements: aim (map the cortex), method (electrical stimulation of awake patients during surgery), results (movements and vivid memories triggered), conclusion (functions are localised). The most common error is giving only the findings without the method or conclusion. For the lobes, a simple memory trick is: the occipital lobe is at the back — “O” for “Occiput” (back of head); frontal is at the front.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The brain has four lobes with distinct functions: frontal (movement, planning), temporal (hearing, language), parietal (touch, senses), occipital (vision), plus the cerebellum (movement coordination) at the base.
  • Specific functional areas include the motor cortex (voluntary movement), somatosensory cortex (touch), visual cortex (sight), auditory cortex (sound), and language areas (Broca’s and Wernicke’s).
  • Penfield’s study (electrical stimulation of awake surgical patients) provided direct evidence for localisation: stimulating the motor cortex caused movements; stimulating the temporal lobe triggered memories.

practice_questions.text:
Which lobe of the brain is primarily responsible for processing visual information?
A) Frontal lobe
B) Parietal lobe
C) Temporal lobe
D) Occipital lobe

practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise definition stating that specific areas of the brain are responsible for specific functions, with a supporting example such as the motor cortex controlling movement or the occipital lobe processing vision [2 marks].
Secure: Core principle correct — different brain areas have different functions — without a supporting example [1 mark].
Developing: Vague reference to different brain areas doing different things [0–1 mark].
Emerging: Incorrect or irrelevant [0 marks].

practice_questions.text: Describe the function of the cerebellum.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per accurate point up to 3 marks. Students may include: located at the back and base of the brain; coordinates smooth and precise movement; involved in balance and motor coordination; involved in procedural learning/acquiring motor skills through practice; without it movements become clumsy and uncoordinated.
Mastering: Location, core function and one additional specific role all stated clearly.
Secure: Location and function stated.
Developing: Function stated without location or vice versa.
Emerging: Vague description only.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Penfield's study provides evidence for localisation of function in the brain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes the method (electrical stimulation of awake patients during surgery), identifies what was found (motor cortex stimulation → movements; temporal lobe stimulation → vivid memories), and explains how this supports localisation (different areas produced different, predictable responses). Two developed, linked points.
Secure: Describes method and links one result to the principle of localisation.
Developing: Describes the study but does not explicitly link results to localisation.
Emerging: Vague reference to Penfield studying the brain without accurate content.

practice_questions.text: Describe Penfield's study of the interpretive cortex, including the aim, method, results and conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each for: aim (to map cortex functions in epilepsy patients during surgery); method (electrical probe applied to the cortex; patients kept awake; responses recorded); results (motor cortex stimulation produced movements; temporal lobe stimulation triggered memories); conclusion (functions are localised to specific cortical areas); naming the temporal lobe region Penfield called the 'interpretive cortex'.
Mastering: All five elements included.
Secure: Four elements.
Developing: Two or three elements.
Emerging: Vague description without accurate AMRC structure.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the localisation of function in the brain, including reference to Penfield's study.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate description of the lobes and their functions (at least three); description of Penfield's study (aim, method, results, conclusion); two elaborated evaluation points (e.g. supported by multiple sources of evidence — strength; complex behaviours involve networks, not single areas — weakness; brain plasticity as a challenge to strict localisation), each developed with reasoning.
Secure: Description of at least two lobes and Penfield's findings; two evaluation points with some development.
Developing: Partial description; one evaluation point.
Emerging: Basic mention of brain areas without functions; evaluation is a single unsupported claim.
[AO1 ~4 marks; AO3 ~5 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which brain structure coordinates smooth, precise movement and balance?
In Penfield's study, what happened when he electrically stimulated the temporal lobe of awake patients?
options: Patients made involuntary movements in specific body parts
Patients reported vivid memories and experiences
Patients lost the ability to speak

knowledge_checks.q: The _____ lobe at the back of the brain is responsible for processing visual information from the eyes.
The somatosensory area, which processes touch and body sensation, is located in the _____ lobe.
Match each brain area to the function it controls.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the main function of the frontal lobe?
flashcard_questions.a: Voluntary movement (motor cortex), planning, decision-making and personality.

flashcard_questions.q: Which lobe processes hearing and is important for language comprehension?
Which lobe processes touch, temperature and pain?
flashcard_questions.a: The parietal lobe (via the somatosensory cortex).

flashcard_questions.q: Which lobe is at the back of the brain and processes vision?

flashcard_questions.a: Coordinates smooth, precise movement and balance.
Specific areas of the brain are responsible for specific functions.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the aim of Penfield's study?
flashcard_questions.a: To map which areas of the cortex are responsible for movement and conscious experience.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of patients did Penfield study, and why were they kept awake?
flashcard_questions.a: Epilepsy patients undergoing surgery — kept awake so they could report what they experienced.

flashcard_questions.q: How did Penfield stimulate the brains of his patients?
flashcard_questions.a: Using an electrical probe during brain surgery, while patients were awake.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Penfield find when he stimulated the motor cortex?
flashcard_questions.a: Involuntary movements in specific body parts — mapped as the motor homunculus.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Penfield find when he stimulated the temporal lobe?
flashcard_questions.a: Patients reported vivid memories and experiences — the 'interpretive cortex'.

flashcard_questions.q: What was Penfield's conclusion about the organisation of the cortex?
flashcard_questions.a: Functions are localised — different areas control different behaviours systematically.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one challenge to the strict localisation of function view.
flashcard_questions.a: Complex behaviours involve networks of areas; brain plasticity allows functions to shift after injury.

glossary_terms.definition: The idea that specific areas of the brain are responsible for particular functions, such as movement, vision or language.
The lobe at the front of the brain, involved in decision-making, planning, personality and voluntary movement.
The lobe at the side of the brain, involved in processing auditory information and language comprehension.
The lobe at the top and back of the brain, involved in processing somatosensory information — touch, pressure, temperature and pain.
The lobe at the very back of the brain, dedicated to processing visual information from the eyes.
A structure at the back and base of the brain that coordinates movement, balance and fine motor skills.
A strip of cortex in the frontal lobe that sends signals to voluntary muscles throughout the body.
A strip of cortex in the parietal lobe that receives sensory signals from the skin and body.
The area in the occipital lobe that receives and processes signals from the eyes.
The area in the temporal lobe that processes sounds from the ears.
